claims.text: A direct two-phase coexistence simulation can accurately compute the melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
The direct two-phase coexistence method has a lower computational cost than full ab initio free-energy integration.
A two-phase simulation cell containing both solid and liquid can be used near the material's melting region.
Ab initio molecular dynamics can monitor solid-liquid interface evolution in a two-phase coexistence setup under constant-pressure conditions.
A sufficiently large simulation cell is needed to avoid significant finite-size effects.
The evolving solid-liquid interface enables extraction of phase-dependent energetic and volumetric data.
At the true melting temperature, a solid-liquid interface is at equilibrium and neither phase grows at the expense of the other.
Energy differences between the coexisting phases can be used to determine the enthalpy of fusion.
Coexistence data can be used to determine the entropy of fusion.
Volume differences between the coexisting phases can be used to determine the volume change at melting.
A stable solid-liquid interface identifies the equilibrium melting temperature.
Full free-energy calculations using thermodynamic integration and ab initio molecular dynamics are highly accurate.
Full ab initio free-energy calculations are too computationally expensive for high-throughput screening.
Two-phase coexistence results may be sensitive to simulation-cell size and interface orientation.
Interface instability, finite-size effects, or sampling errors may cause discrepancies in predicted melting properties.
Agreement with full free-energy methods may vary with simulation-cell size and the selected DFT functional.
